segments.description: Please welcome Sean Malcolm, a dedicated tennis coach with 18 years of experience supporting players, coaches and programs. With a background in sports science and sports psychology from Laubara University and currently pursuing a PhD in coaching and skill acquisition, Sean is passionate about creating environments, the foster, player wellbeing and performance. Today he'll present preparing our players for the match court, sharing strategies to help players excel under competitive pressure. Let's welcome Sean. Hello everyone, I'm Sean Malcolm, a tennis coach based out of London, UK. I run a tennis program called Infinite Tennis, which cares for players 13 to 18 years old. I've recently embarked on a PhD program with Professor Keith Davids at Sheffield Hallam University, researching the constraint-led approach. Today I'm really excited to be here and share a bit about my journey and how my academic research influences my practical work with this theme of preparing our players for the match court and being curious about what effects does our practice design have on the learners who are interacting with them. I'll briefly go over three key ideas from the academia which guide my practice and then we'll get into some of the practical side. The first idea that really caught me is this representative learning design. This really gets to the heart of the transfer problem. How much of our training is transferring over to the competitive environment

and the idea that possibly not all repetitions are equal, so some offer maybe a higher learning value than others, so it makes you think can we squeeze a little bit more at our practice time. I think also representative learning design is really interested in developing adaptable players, adaptable problem solvers who can deal with multiple different situations in their future tennis, which I'm very interested and curious about. Lastly, as a lot of the training is competitive, we get emotion and players have to deal with that and improve their competitive behaviors in response to that. Secondly, I'd like to introduce the idea that information and movement is a relationship as James Gibson, the ecological psychologist, spoke about. This is an ongoing relationship where players have the ability to adapt to changing conditions. This could be at the short timescale of the ball coming over the net, for example taking a bad bounce and me being able to adapt and still get the ball back and then also at longer timescales possibly over the course of a match as I start to pick up information about where a player serves or even over a season where players co-adapt to each other to learn how to win and how to beat each other. In this sense, skillful behavior is how tuned in I am to this information and relationship. Here's a great clip of Dan Evans showing this idea.
